weeks.title: Folders and paths — knowing where a file really lives

lesson.title: Folders and paths — knowing where a file really lives
lesson.body_md: Help card DCO-3101: Ana saved a summer photo and the file dialog now says 'not found'. Every file has an address called a path, written from the top of the drive down through folders, like /home/ana/Documents/photos/summer.jpg. That full form is an absolute path because it starts at the root, the single slash. Programs also accept relative paths that start from wherever you are standing, called the current working directory. Two dots mean the folder above, and a single dot means here. Standing in /home/ana/Documents/letters, the relative path ../photos/2026/../summer.jpg climbs out of letters into Documents, steps into photos and into 2026, then climbs back out of 2026, landing on /home/ana/Documents/photos/summer.jpg. Walk it with your finger on a drawn tree before trusting it. Windows writes C:\Users\Ana\Documents with backslashes and a drive letter, but the idea of climbing and descending is the same. When a file goes missing, ask two questions out loud: where am I standing, and which way does the path walk from here.

weeks.title: Storage units — why a 500 GB drive shows 465 GiB

lesson.title: Storage units — why a 500 GB drive shows 465 GiB
lesson.body_md: DCO-3202 is a NO_AI week; work the division on paper. A patron bought a '500 GB' drive and thinks the store cheated her because the computer shows about 465 GB. Nobody cheated. Drive makers count in powers of ten, so a gigabyte is 1,000,000,000 bytes. Many operating systems count in powers of two, where a gibibyte, GiB, is 1,073,741,824 bytes, and then label the result GB anyway. Divide 500,000,000,000 by 1,073,741,824 and you get about 465.66, the same drive described in a bigger unit. The same confusion bites when deciding whether something will fit. Her phone holds 1,200 photos at about 4.2 MB each, where MB means a million bytes, so the folder is 5.04 billion bytes. In the binary unit that is about 4.69 GiB, and the laptop says 4.5 GiB free. It will not fit, even though '5 GB into 4.5' felt close. Write the unit beside every number, convert both sides to the same unit before comparing, and leave room to spare, because a completely full disk makes most computers slow and unstable.
lesson.worked_example: 500 GB = 500×10^9 B = 465.66 GiB; 1,200 photos × 4.2 MB = 5.04×10^9 B = 4.694 GiB > 4.5 GiB free → does not fit

weeks.title: Passwords and passphrases — strength is length times choice

lesson.title: Passwords and passphrases — strength is length times choice
lesson.body_md: DCO-3303 starts with a sticky note that says P@ssw0rd! and a question: is this strong? Strength depends on how the password was chosen, not on how it looks. If every character is picked at random from a pool, the number of possibilities is the pool size raised to the length, and we measure it in bits: length times log2 of the pool. Four words drawn at random from a 7,776-word dice list give about 51.7 bits. Eight characters drawn at random from the 95 printable keyboard symbols give about 52.6 bits. Twelve random lowercase letters give about 56.4 bits, stronger than either, because length grows strength faster than adding symbols. P@ssw0rd! scores far lower than its nine characters suggest, because guessing tools try dictionary words with common swaps first. The NIST digital identity guidance, SP 800-63B, favours long memorable secrets, checking them against lists of known-breached passwords, and changing them when there is evidence of compromise rather than on a fixed calendar. Use a different secret on every site, and let a password manager remember them.
lesson.worked_example: 4 diceware words: 4×log2(7776) = 51.70 bits; 8 random printable: 8×log2(95) = 52.56; 12 random lowercase: 12×log2(26) = 56.41

weeks.title: Reading a link — the real address is at the right end

lesson.title: Reading a link — the real address is at the right end
lesson.body_md: DCO-3404 is a text message that says a bank account is locked and offers a link. Before tapping, read the address the way a computer does. Skip the https:// and stop at the first single slash after it; what sits between is the hostname. Read the hostname from the right end, label by label, because the rightmost labels say who owns it. In https://account.harborbank.example.verify-login.example.net/session the hostname is account.harborbank.example.verify-login.example.net, and its last two labels are example.net. The bank's name near the left is just decoration chosen by whoever owns example.net, which is not the bank. So the call is: do not open. Real organisations rarely ask you to log in from a message; type the bank's address yourself or use its app. Some country endings use three labels, such as .co.uk, so the rule 'last two labels' is a starting point, and the course's examples use the reserved .example endings so nobody is sent anywhere real. When unsure, show the message to the library desk rather than replying.
lesson.worked_example: https://account.harborbank.example.verify-login.example.net/session → hostname ends in example.net → not harborbank.example → do not open

weeks.title: Spreadsheet formulas — let the sheet do the arithmetic

lesson.title: Spreadsheet formulas — let the sheet do the arithmetic
lesson.body_md: DCO-3505 is a monthly budget written on the back of an envelope that never adds up the same way twice. Move it into a spreadsheet: labels in column A, amounts in column B, one row per item. Rent is 650, food 240, the bus pass 55, the phone 35, and savings 120. Instead of typing the total, write =SUM(B2:B6) and the sheet answers 1,100, then keeps answering correctly when the phone bill changes. =AVERAGE(B2:B6) gives 220, the typical line, and =MAX(B2:B6) finds the largest amount, which belongs to rent. To see how much of the month food takes, divide its cell by the total cell, =B3/B7, and format the result as a percentage: about 21.82 percent. The habit worth keeping is that numbers you typed live in one place and every other number is a formula pointing at them. A total typed by hand goes stale the first time anything changes, and that is how budgets quietly stop matching reality. Save the file somewhere you will find it, with a name that says what and when.
lesson.worked_example: rent 650, food 240, bus pass 55, phone 35, savings 120 → =SUM 1100, =AVERAGE 220, =MAX rent, food share =240/1100 = 21.82%

weeks.title: Keyboard fluency — gross speed, net speed, accuracy

lesson.title: Keyboard fluency — gross speed, net speed, accuracy
lesson.body_md: DCO-3606 is a NO_AI week because it measures your own hands. Job applications and online forms reward people who can type steadily, so the library runs a five-minute practice passage. Typing speed is counted in words per minute, where a 'word' is defined as five characters, spaces included, so long and short words count fairly. Typing 1,250 characters in five minutes is 250 'words' over five minutes, a gross speed of 50 WPM. Mistakes left uncorrected are subtracted per minute: fifteen errors over five minutes costs three, so net speed is 47 WPM. Accuracy compares correct characters with all characters, 1,235 out of 1,250, or 98.8 percent. Most learners improve fastest by slowing down until accuracy stays near ninety-eight percent, then letting speed return, because unlearning a mistyped pattern takes longer than learning it right. Sit square to the keyboard, keep wrists level, and rest the index fingers on the small bumps on F and J. Record the three numbers each week rather than chasing a single best run.
lesson.worked_example: 1,250 characters in 5 minutes with 15 uncorrected errors → gross 50 WPM, net 47 WPM, accuracy 98.8%

weeks.title: Attachments — why a 19 MB file will not fit under 25 MB

lesson.title: Attachments — why a 19 MB file will not fit under 25 MB
lesson.body_md: DCO-3707: a patron's resume portfolio is 19 MB, the mail service says attachments up to 25 MB, and sending still fails. Email was designed to carry text, so attachments are converted into text with an encoding called base64 before they travel. Base64 turns every three bytes into four characters, so the encoded file is about a third larger: four times the byte count divided by three, rounded up to a whole group. Nineteen million bytes become 25,333,336 bytes, just over the 25,000,000-byte limit, which is why the message bounces even though the file looked small enough. An 18 MB file would encode to 24,000,000 bytes and squeak through. When something will not fit, do not split it into a dozen emails or squeeze the quality until the pictures blur. Upload it to a storage service, share a link with view-only permission, and mention in the message what the link is and how long it will stay up. Never attach other people's personal documents to practice messages; the lab uses only made-up byte counts.

weeks.title: Backups — three copies, two kinds of storage, one away from home

lesson.title: Backups — three copies, two kinds of storage, one away from home
lesson.body_md: DCO-3808 begins with tears: a laptop died and took two years of family photos with it. A simple rule, called 3-2-1, prevents most of these stories. Keep three copies of anything you would miss, the original plus two backups. Store them on at least two different kinds of storage, so one failure type, such as a batch of bad drives, cannot take everything. Keep one copy somewhere else, away from the house, so a fire, flood, or theft leaves something behind. The library's example plan has the photos on the laptop's SSD, a copy on a USB hard drive at home, and a copy in a cloud folder; that is three copies, three kinds of storage, and one offsite. There is a fourth rule people forget: a backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan. Once a month, pick a random file and open it from each backup. Two copies on the same USB stick are one copy with extra steps, and a sync folder that mirrors deletions instantly is convenient but is not a backup on its own.
lesson.worked_example: laptop SSD + home USB HDD + cloud folder (offsite) → 3 copies, 3 media, 1 offsite; restore tested → plan_ok

lesson.title: Readable screens — measuring colour contrast
lesson.body_md: DCO-3909: the library's new event flyer uses pale grey text, and a patron with low vision cannot read it. Readability can be measured. The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, WCAG 2.2, define a contrast ratio between text and background colours. Each colour's red, green, and blue values are converted to a relative luminance, a weighted brightness in which green counts most and blue least, and the ratio is the lighter luminance plus 0.05 divided by the darker luminance plus 0.05. Black on white is 21 to 1; identical colours are 1 to 1. Normal-size text needs at least 4.5 to 1 for level AA, and large text needs 3 to 1. The grey #767676 on white measures about 4.54 and just passes. One step lighter, #777777, measures about 4.48 and fails for normal text, even though most eyes cannot tell the two apart, which is exactly why you measure rather than guess. Use a contrast checker before printing or posting, and remember contrast is one accessibility check among many, not the whole job.
lesson.worked_example: #767676 on #ffffff → 4.54:1 passes AA normal text; #777777 on #ffffff → 4.48:1 fails AA normal, passes AA large

weeks.title: Personal digital safety plan — the page you keep

lesson.title: Personal digital safety plan — the page you keep
lesson.body_md: DCO-3A10 asks each learner to leave the Library Lab with one page they will actually use. It names a password manager, because unique secrets for every site are impossible to remember otherwise. It turns on multi-factor sign-in for the email account first, since email is where every other password reset arrives, so whoever controls it controls the rest. It lists the backup copies by media and location, passes the 3-2-1 rule, and records the date of the last test restore. It names a real person or desk to show strange messages to, such as the library's IT desk, so nobody has to judge a convincing scam alone at midnight. It records which colours and font sizes work for the reader's eyes. It never contains an actual password, PIN, or recovery code; those belong in the manager or on paper locked away, not on a page that might be photographed. Mentors check the plan against six or more passed labs and ask the learner to show one step live, such as opening a file from the cloud backup.
lesson.worked_example: password manager yes; MFA on email yes; laptop/USB/cloud backups with tested restore; report phishing to the library IT desk; no real passwords in the plan
